mainTopic: A series of אגדה teachings of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: אברהם and 'אדון', the meaning of names, challenging רשעים, a fixed place for תפילה, and serving תלמידי חכמים
overview: This amud is a long series of teachings that רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי. אברהם was the first to call הקב"ה 'אדון', and רב adds that דניאל's תפילה was answered in that merit. We should not try to calm a person while he is still angry. לאה was the first to thank הקב"ה, and this leads the גמרא to explain the names ראובן and רות and to show that a name affects a person (שמא גרים). A wayward child at home is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג, which is why דוד called his escape from אבשלום a מזמור, a song. It is permitted to challenge רשעים, and the גמרא gives several ways to fit this with רבי יצחק's warning not to provoke a רשע whose luck is shining. The amud also teaches that a fixed place for תפילה makes one's enemies fall, and that serving a תלמיד חכם is greater than learning from him. It ends with a story in which רבי יצחק urges רב נחמן to daven with the צבור, and the reason he gives continues on the next amud.

steps.title: אברהם was the first to call הקב"ה 'אדון'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that no one called הקב"ה 'אדון' until אברהם did. He proves it from a פסוק in בראשית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: From the day הקב"ה created the world, no person called Him 'Master,' until אברהם came and called Him Master. As the פסוק says: 'And he said, My Lord God, how will I know that I will inherit it?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new set of teachings from רבי שמעון בן יוחי. The first one praises אברהם for being the first to call הקב"ה 'אדון'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Calling ה׳‎ 'אדון' means seeing Him as the Master and Owner of everything, not only as the Creator. The proof is בראשית ט"ו:ח, where אברהם opens his words with 'אדני' (my Master). This is the first time the Torah shows a person speaking to ה׳ with that name.

keyTerms.meaning: In the name of. It shows who first said the teaching.
Master or Lord. It means ה׳ is the Owner who is in charge.
As it is said. It introduces a פסוק as proof.
My Master. This is the name of ה׳ that אברהם used.

steps.whyThisMatters: This idea is the foundation for רב's next teaching. Because the name 'אדני' is tied to אברהם, using that name can call up his merit.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
phrases.notes: This opens a new series. Until now the גמרא quoted רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי.

phrases.aramaic: מִיּוֹם שֶׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: From the day that the Holy One, Blessed be He, created the world,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא הָיָה אָדָם שֶׁקְּרָאוֹ לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״אָדוֹן״,
phrases.english: there was no person who called the Holy One, Blessed be He, 'Master,'
until Abraham came and called Him Master,
as it is said: 'And he said: My Lord, God,'
'by what shall I know that I will inherit it?'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new series of teachings from רבי שמעון בן יוחי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אברהם was the first person to call הקב"ה 'אדון', as shown in בראשית ט"ו:ח.

steps.title: דניאל was answered in אברהם's merit
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that even דניאל's תפילה was answered only because of אברהם. He quotes a פסוק from דניאל that ends with 'for the sake of אדני'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Even דניאל was answered only because of אברהם. As the פסוק says: 'And now, listen, our God, to the prayer of Your servant and to his pleas, and shine Your face upon Your desolate מקדש, for the sake of the Lord.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב builds on the last teaching and claims that דניאל's תפילה was accepted in the merit of אברהם. He quotes the פסוק, and the next step will show why this פסוק proves his point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key words are at the end of the פסוק: 'למען אדני' (for the sake of the Lord). At this point, רב has only quoted the פסוק. The proof depends on noticing that this wording is strange, which the גמרא explains next.

keyTerms.meaning: Even. It shows this case goes further than the previous idea.
Was answered. His תפילה was accepted.
Because of, or in the merit of.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: אַף דָּנִיאֵל לֹא נַעֲנָה
phrases.english: Rav said: Even Daniel was not answered
except on account of Abraham,
as it is said: 'And now listen, our God,'
'to the prayer of Your servant and to his supplications,'
'and cause Your face to shine upon Your desolate Sanctuary'
'for the sake of the Lord.'
phrases.notes: This is the key phrase for the proof.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: אַף דָּנִיאֵל לֹא נַעֲנָה אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל אַבְרָהָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 1: since אברהם is linked to the name 'אדון', that name can call up his merit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דניאל's תפילה was answered in the merit of אברהם.

steps.title: The verse should have said 'for Your sake'
steps.stepSummary: The wording of the פסוק is strange. דניאל is speaking directly to ה׳, so he should have said 'למענך' (for Your sake), not 'למען אדני' (for the sake of the Lord).
steps.simpleTranslation: It should have said 'for Your sake'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a problem in the wording of the פסוק. This sets up the answer that completes רב's proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דניאל is talking to ה׳ in the second person ('listen,' 'Your servant,' 'Your face'). Then he suddenly switches to the third person, 'for the sake of the Lord.' This change suggests that 'אדני' must mean something extra.

keyTerms.meaning: It should have said. This shows we expected different wording.

steps.confusionAlert: This is not an attack on רב. The question is part of רב's own proof: the strange wording is exactly what shows the hint to אברהם.

phrases.english: It should have said 'for Your sake.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the פסוק quoted in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'למען אדני' in דניאל ט':י"ז.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: דניאל speaks to ה׳ directly, so the natural wording would be 'למענך'. The switch to 'אדני' needs an explanation.

steps.title: 'למען אדני' means for אברהם's sake
steps.stepSummary: 'למען אדני' means 'for the sake of the one who called You אדון', that is, אברהם. This completes רב's proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means: for the sake of אברהם, who called You 'Master.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the wording problem. 'אדני' is a hint to אברהם, so דניאל was asking to be answered in אברהם's merit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 taught that אברהם was the first to call ה׳‎ 'אדון'. So when דניאל says 'for the sake of אדני', he is saying 'for the sake of the one who gave You that name.' This proves רב's claim that דניאל was answered because of אברהם.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. It introduces the correct reading.

steps.whatToRemember: אברהם was the first to call ה׳‎ 'אדון'. Because of that, the name 'אדני' carries his merit, and even דניאל was answered through it.

phrases.english: Rather, it means for the sake of Abraham, who called You 'Master.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording problem raised in step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word in the פסוק as a hint.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'אדני' simply means ה׳, which makes the wording seem strange.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'אדני' points to אברהם, the first to call ה׳‎ 'אדון', so the prayer asks for his merit.

steps.title: Do not try to calm a person while he is angry
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, again quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, asks for the source that one should not try to appease a person in the middle of his anger. He answers with a פסוק from שמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: From where do we know that we do not try to appease a person while he is angry? As it is said: 'My face will go, and I will give you rest.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new teaching in the same series from רבי שמעון בן יוחי. This one is about not trying to calm someone during his anger, and it gives a פסוק as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This topic is new and is not connected to אברהם. The פסוק (שמות ל"ג:י"ד) is ה׳ speaking to משה after the sin of the golden calf. The words 'My face will go' are understood to mean: wait until My angry face passes, and then I will give you rest.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? It asks for a source.
At the time of his anger, while he is still angry.
And I will give rest or calm.

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a practical lesson for how people treat each other. Trying to calm someone at the peak of his anger usually fails, so it is better to wait until the anger passes.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
From where do we know that one does not appease a person
at the time of his anger?
As it is said: 'My face will go, and I will give you rest.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, unrelated teaching in the same series from רבי שמעון בן יוחי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One should not try to appease a person while he is still angry. The source is 'פני ילכו והנחתי לך'.

steps.title: לאה was the first person to thank הקב"ה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that from the time the world was created, no one thanked הקב"ה until לאה did. The proof is a פסוק about the birth of יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: From the day הקב"ה created His world, no person thanked Him, until לאה came and thanked Him. As it says: 'This time I will thank ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching from the same chain, רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי. It says לאה was the first person ever to thank הקב"ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern as Step 1, where אברהם was the first to call הקב"ה 'אדון'. Here, לאה is the first to give הודאה (thanks). The proof is that when יהודה was born she said 'הפעם אודה', meaning 'this time I will thank', and she named him יהודה from that word.

keyTerms.meaning: I will thank (the root of the name יְהוּדָה)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't take this to mean nobody before לאה was ever grateful. The point is that she was the first to openly name and express thanks to הקב"ה in this way.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:

phrases.aramaic: מִיּוֹם שֶׁבָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת עוֹלָמוֹ
phrases.english: From the day the Holy One, Blessed be He, created His world

phrases.aramaic: לֹא הָיָה אָדָם שֶׁהוֹדָה לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: there was no person who thanked the Holy One, Blessed be He,
until Leah came and thanked Him,
phrases.notes: She gave thanks at the birth of her fourth son.

phrases.english: as it says: 'This time I will thank ה׳.'
phrases.notes: בראשית כט:לה. This is why the child is named יהודה.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another teaching in the same chain of רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, built on the 'first person to...' pattern from Step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לאה was the first person to thank הקב"ה, as shown by 'הפעם אודה את ה׳'.

steps.title: The meaning of ראובן's name: עשו hated יעקב even after selling willingly
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains the name ראובן as 'ראו מה בין בני לבן חמי', meaning 'see the difference between my son and my father-in-law's son.' He begins with עשו: even though עשו sold his בכורה willingly, he still hated יעקב.
steps.simpleTranslation: ראובן. רבי אלעזר said: לאה said, 'See the difference between my son and the son of my father-in-law.' My father-in-law's son, עשו, sold his בכורה willingly, as it says 'He sold his birthright to יעקב.' Yet look what is written about him: 'And עשו hated יעקב.'
steps.whatsHappening: Because the גמרא just explained יהודה's name, it moves on to another son of לאה, ראובן. רבי אלעזר starts building a comparison, and here he gives the first side: עשו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name ראובן is read as two words: 'ראו' (see) and 'בן' (son). לאה is pointing out a contrast between her son and עשו, the son of her father-in-law יצחק. עשו sold the בכורה by his own free choice, yet he still hated יעקב over it.

keyTerms.meaning: Reuben, read here as 'רְאוּ בֵּן', meaning 'see, a son'
The son of my father-in-law, meaning עֵשָׂו, son of יִצְחָק
And he hated / held a grudge

steps.confusionAlert: 'בן חמי' is not לאה's own relative by blood. חמי means 'my father-in-law' (יצחק), so his son is עשו.

phrases.english: Reuben.
phrases.notes: A heading: now the גמרא explains this name.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרָה לֵאָה: רְאוּ מָה בֵּין בְּנִי לְבֶן חָמִי.
phrases.english: Leah said: See what the difference is between my son and the son of my father-in-law.
For whereas the son of my father-in-law (Esau),

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּמִדַּעְתֵּיהּ זַבְּנַיהּ לִבְכֵירוּתֵיהּ,
phrases.english: even though he sold his birthright of his own will,
as it is written: 'And he sold his birthright to Jacob,'
see what is written about him:
'And Esau hated Jacob.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side-topic: after explaining יהודה's name, the גמרא explains the name of another son of לאה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The name ראובן means 'see the difference.' עשו sold his בכורה willingly and still hated יעקב.

steps.title: Proof that עשו's hatred was also about the בכורה
steps.stepSummary: A second פסוק shows that עשו's anger was not only about the ברכות. He also complained about the בכורה, which he himself had sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'He said: Is he not rightly named יעקב, for he has tricked me twice.' (He took my birthright, and now he took my blessing.)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second פסוק to support the first side of the comparison. It shows that עשו's hatred was really connected to the בכורה too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might say 'וישטם עשו' was only about the stolen ברכות. This פסוק proves otherwise: עשו counts the בכורה as one of the two times יעקב 'tricked' him, even though he had sold it willingly. That strengthens the claim that עשו resented something he gave up by his own choice.

keyTerms.meaning: And he tricked me / went around me (same root as יַעֲקֹב)
Etc.: the פסוק continues beyond what is quoted

steps.confusionAlert: The proof is mainly in the part hidden under 'וגו׳': 'את בכרתי לקח' (he took my birthright). That part is what ties עשו's anger to the בכורה.

phrases.english: And it is written: 'And he said: Is he not rightly named Jacob,'
'for he has tricked me these two times,' etc.
phrases.notes: בראשית כז:לו. It continues: 'he took my birthright, and now he took my blessing.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports Step 7 by showing that עשו's hatred included resentment over the בכורה.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that עשו hated יעקב because of the בכורה he had willingly sold.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית כז:לו: 'ויעקבני זה פעמים... את בכרתי לקח'.

steps.title: ראובן lost his בכורה by force but was not jealous
steps.stepSummary: The other side of the contrast: ראובן lost his בכורה to יוסף against his will, yet he was not jealous. He even saved יוסף from the brothers.
steps.simpleTranslation: But my son: even though יוסף took his בכורה from him against his will, as it says 'Because he defiled his father's bed, his birthright was given to the sons of יוסף,' even so he was not jealous of him. As it says: 'And ראובן heard, and he saved him from their hands.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר finishes the comparison by describing ראובן. This is the 'see the difference' that the name ראובן points to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The contrast is sharp. עשו gave up his בכורה willingly and still hated. ראובן had his בכורה taken by force and still did not envy יוסף. The proof that he held no jealousy is that ראובן tried to save יוסף's life.
steps.whatToRemember: ראובן = 'ראו בן' (see the son). עשו sold his בכורה willingly and still hated יעקב. ראובן lost his בכורה by force and still saved יוסף. The name itself praises ראובן's good heart.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how חז"ל read names in the תורה as hidden messages. It also gives a model of rising above jealousy, even when you have truly lost something.

phrases.english: Whereas my son (Reuben),
even though against his will
Joseph took his birthright from him,
as it is written: 'And because he defiled his father's bed,'
'his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph,'
even so, he was not jealous of him,
as it is written: 'And Reuben heard, and he saved him from their hands.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִילּוּ בְּנִי, אַף עַל גַּב דְּעַל כֻּרְחֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the comparison begun in Step 7 by presenting ראובן as the opposite of עשו.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The name ראובן highlights the difference: עשו resented a בכורה he sold willingly, while ראובן was not jealous of יוסף even after losing his בכורה by force, and he even saved him.

steps.title: What does the name רות mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא continues the topic of names and asks what the name רות means.
steps.simpleTranslation: רות: what is the meaning of the name 'רות'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. Right after explaining the name ראובן, it asks what the name רות hints at.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We just saw that the name ראובן carried a hidden message. The גמרא now applies the same approach to another biblical name, רות. It treats a name as something that can hint at a person's destiny.

keyTerms.meaning: What is / what does it mean
Ruth, the Moabite convert and ancestor of דוד

phrases.english: Ruth: what is the meaning of 'Ruth'?
phrases.notes: Continues the series of name explanations that began with ראובן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the explanation of the name ראובן to the name רות.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What hidden meaning is in the name רות?

steps.title: רות's name hints at דוד, who saturated הקב"ה with songs
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that רות merited to have דוד descend from her. דוד 'saturated' הקב"ה with songs and praises, and רות sounds like the word for saturating (ריוה).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Because she merited that דוד came from her, who saturated הקב"ה with songs and praises.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question. The name רות hints at her great descendant דוד, who poured out songs of praise to הקב"ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer works on sound. The letters ר-ו of רות match ריוהו, meaning 'he saturated Him'. So רות's name already pointed to the תהלים her descendant דוד would write.

keyTerms.meaning: That he saturated / filled Him to the full (from רוה)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
That she merited that David came out from her
who saturated the Holy One, Blessed be He
phrases.notes: ריוהו (saturated) sounds like רות. This is the wordplay.

phrases.english: with songs and praises.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: שֶׁזָּכְתָה וְיָצָא מִמֶּנָּה דָּוִד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רות's name hints that דוד, who saturated הקב"ה with songs and praises (ריוהו), would come from her.

steps.title: What is the source that a name affects a person?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the basis of the whole idea behind these explanations: that a person's name actually has an effect on his life.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know that the name has an effect?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps back and asks a basic question. How do we know that a name really influences a person's future?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The explanations of ראובן and רות assume that a name is not random but shapes or predicts a life. Before going further, the גמרא wants a פסוק that supports this assumption.

keyTerms.meaning: A name has an effect / a name causes

phrases.english: From where do we know that the name has an effect?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind the name explanations in steps 7 and 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A scriptural source that names affect a person's life.

steps.title: Read the verse as 'names' instead of 'desolations'
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר brings a פסוק from תהלים: 'Go see the works of ה׳, who has placed שַׁמּוֹת in the land.' He reads שַׁמּוֹת (desolations) as שֵׁמוֹת (names). So names are among ה׳'s works in the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר said: For the פסוק says: 'Go, see the works of ה׳, who has placed desolations (שַׁמּוֹת) in the land.' Do not read 'שַׁמּוֹת' (desolations), but 'שֵׁמוֹת' (names).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר answers the question with a פסוק. By re-reading one word, the פסוק now says that ה׳ 'places names in the land'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain meaning of the פסוק is 'desolations'. The re-reading turns the same letters into 'names', which makes names one of ה׳'s deliberate 'works'. Since ה׳ directs them, a name carries real meaning for a person's life.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not read it as ... but as ... (a re-reading for a דרשה)

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תקרי' does not mean the text of the פסוק is wrong or should be changed. It adds a second layer of meaning on top of the plain reading.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer said: for the verse says:
'Go, see the works of ה׳,
who has placed desolations in the land.'
Do not read 'shamot' (desolations), but rather 'shemot' (names).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 12 with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: From תהלים מו:ט, re-read as 'who placed names in the land'. Names are ה׳'s works.
steps.whatToRemember: שמא גרים: a name has an effect. The source is 'אשר שם שמות בארץ', read as שֵׁמוֹת (names). This is the basis for the name explanations of ראובן and רות.

steps.title: A wayward child at home is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that תרבות רעה (a child who goes bad) inside a person's home is harder than the great war of גוג ומגוג.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: Bad upbringing (a wayward child) within a person's house is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the series of teachings from רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי. This new teaching is about how painful a wayward child is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The war of גוג ומגוג is the most frightening war of the end of days. Even so, רבי שמעון בן יוחי says trouble from one's own child at home hurts more. The proof follows in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Bad upbringing, a child who has gone bad
The great war of the end of days

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:
phrases.notes: The same chain of tradition as in steps 5–6.

phrases.aramaic: קָשָׁה תַּרְבּוּת רָעָה בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם
phrases.english: A wayward upbringing within a person's house is harder
than the war of Gog and Magog.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching in the series of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wayward child in one's home is harder to bear than the war of גוג ומגוג.

steps.title: Proof from comparing תהלים ג with תהלים ב
steps.stepSummary: In תהלים ג, when דוד fled from his son אבשלום, he cried 'ה׳, how many are my enemies!' In תהלים ב, about the war of גוג ומגוג, he says only 'Why are the nations in an uproar?' and does not say 'how many are my enemies.' So the trouble from אבשלום was worse.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'A song of דוד, when he fled from אבשלום his son,' and right after it is written: 'ה׳, how many are my enemies, many rise against me.' But regarding the war of גוג ומגוג it is written: 'Why are the nations in an uproar, and the peoples speak emptiness?' And 'how many are my enemies' is not written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves רבי שמעון בן יוחי's claim by comparing two chapters of תהלים. דוד speaks with much more distress about אבשלום than about גוג ומגוג.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With אבשלום, דוד cries out about how many his enemies are, which shows great pain. With גוג ומגוג, the tone is calm, almost dismissive: 'why are they bothering, it is empty.' The missing cry in תהלים ב shows that a rebellious son is the heavier trouble.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is written right after it

phrases.english: As it is said: 'A song of David,'
when he fled from Absalom his son.'
And it is written right after it:
'ה׳, how many are my enemies,'
'many rise up against me.'

phrases.aramaic: וְאִילּוּ גַּבֵּי מִלְחֶמֶת גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג, כְּתִיב:
phrases.english: Whereas regarding the war of Gog and Magog, it is written:
'Why are the nations in an uproar,'
'and the peoples speak emptiness?'
Yet 'how many are my enemies' is not written.
phrases.notes: The point of the proof: the cry of distress is missing in the גוג ומגוג chapter.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד בְּבָרְחוֹ מִפְּנֵי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the proof for the claim in step 14.
steps.raayaObject: That a wayward child (אבשלום) is harder than the war of גוג ומגוג.
steps.raayaSupportSource: תהלים ג:א-ב compared with תהלים ב:א. 'מה רבו צרי' appears only regarding אבשלום.
steps.whatToRemember: A wayward child is worse than גוג ומגוג. The proof: about אבשלום, דוד cried 'מה רבו צרי'. About גוג ומגוג, he did not.

steps.title: Why is it called a song and not a lament?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised by the opening words of תהלים ג. If דוד was running from his own son, why does the פסוק call it 'a song of David'? It should say 'a lament of David'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A song of David, when he fled from Absalom his son': 'A song of David'?! It should have said 'A lament of David'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a difficulty with the title of the chapter it just quoted. It is setting up an answer that will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous step showed that fleeing from אבשלום was a terrible trouble, even worse than גוג ומגוג. So the word מזמור, a joyful song, seems out of place. Sad words like קינה would fit better.

keyTerms.meaning: A lament, a song of mourning

phrases.english: 'A song of David, when he fled from Absalom his son.'
phrases.notes: The גמרא physically repeats the פסוק here to question it, which is a new purpose.

phrases.english: 'A song of David'?!
It should have said 'A lament of David'!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד? קִינָה לְדָוִד מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the פסוק that served as the proof in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The title 'מזמור לדוד' in תהלים ג:א.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A chapter about the painful flight from one's own rebellious son should be called a lament (קינה), not a song (מזמור).

steps.title: A parable about a debt that gets paid
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אבישלום begins answering the question from step 16 with a parable. A man owes money and is worried until he pays, then he is happy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אבישלום said: Here is a משל. What is this like? A man has a שטר חוב (debt document) against him. Before he pays it, he is sad. After he pays it, he is happy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer to the question 'why מזמור?' by telling a parable. It is setting up the next step, where the parable is applied to דוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that a punishment you know is coming feels heavy until it actually happens. Once it is over, a person can feel relief, even joy. The next step shows how this fits דוד.

keyTerms.meaning: A debt document that says a person owes money

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Avishalom said:
A parable: what is this matter like?
To a person who had a debt document issued against him.
Before he paid it, he was sad,
after he paid it, he was happy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to the question of why the פסוק says מזמור.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parable that shows relief after a dreaded event
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Running from a son can only bring sorrow, so the right word would be קינה.
steps.terutzMaskana: When a dreaded punishment finally comes, the worry ends, and that can bring happiness.

steps.title: Applying the parable to דוד and אבשלום
steps.stepSummary: When נתן הנביא told דוד that trouble would come from his own house, דוד feared it would be a slave or a ממזר who would have no mercy. When he saw it was his own son אבשלום, he was glad, so he said מזמור.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too with דוד. When הקב"ה told him, 'I will bring trouble on you from your own house,' he was sad. He said: Maybe it will be a slave or a ממזר, who will have no pity on me. Once he saw it was אבשלום, he was happy. That is why he said 'מזמור', a song.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the debt parable to דוד and finishes answering why the פסוק says מזמור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'debt' is the punishment that ה׳ promised through נתן. דוד worried that a stranger with no feelings for him would carry it out. A son would still have some mercy for his father, so finding out it was אבשלום was like paying the debt in the easiest way. That relief is why he sang.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I will bring trouble on you from your own house' (שמואל ב יב, יא)
A child born from a forbidden relationship

steps.whatToRemember: דוד sang because the punishment came in the mildest way: through a son, who would still have some mercy, not through a stranger.
steps.confusionAlert: דוד was not happy that his son rebelled. He was relieved that the promised punishment came from someone who would still pity him.

phrases.english: So too David,

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא:
phrases.english: once the Holy One, Blessed be He, told him:
'I will raise up trouble against you from your house,'
phrases.notes: Said through נתן הנביא after the story with בת שבע.

phrases.english: he was sad. He said:
Maybe it will be a slave or a mamzer,
who will have no pity on me.
Once he saw that it was Avshalom, he was happy.
That is why he said 'a song.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the parable from step 17 to דוד.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Applying the parable to the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The word מזמור does not fit a time of running from one's son.
steps.terutzMaskana: דוד was relieved that the punishment came through his son, who would pity him, so he sang a מזמור.

steps.title: It is permitted to stand up against the wicked
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that a person may challenge רשעים in this world. He proves it from a פסוק in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: It is permitted to fight against רשעים in this world, as it says: 'Those who leave the תורה praise the wicked, and those who keep the תורה fight them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from the same pair of רבי יוחנן and רבי שמעון בן יוחי: one may challenge רשעים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One could think it is dangerous or wrong to challenge רשעים while they are successful. The פסוק describes שומרי תורה as people who fight them, which shows this is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: To challenge, to provoke, to stand up against

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
It is permitted to provoke the wicked in this world,
as it says: 'Those who leave the Torah praise the wicked,
and those who keep the Torah fight them.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching from the same chain of רבי יוחנן quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, like step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is permitted to challenge רשעים in this world, based on משלי כח, ד.

steps.title: A ברייתא teaches the same thing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that a ברייתא says the same idea, in the name of רבי דוסתאי בר רבי מתון, with the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא: רבי דוסתאי בר רבי מתון says: It is permitted to fight against רשעים in this world, as it says: 'Those who leave the תורה praise the wicked,' etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports רבי יוחנן's teaching with a ברייתא that says the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תניא נמי הכי means an older source, a ברייתא, already says this idea. That makes רבי יוחנן's teaching stronger. The ברייתא also goes on to deal with an objection, which comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way in a ברייתא
'And so on', the rest of the פסוק

phrases.english: It was also taught this way:
Rabbi Dostai son of Rabbi Matun says:
It is permitted to provoke the wicked in this world,
as it says: 'Those who leave the Torah praise the wicked,' and so on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 19 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's rule that one may challenge רשעים
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי דוסתאי בר רבי מתון

steps.title: A verse that seems to say: don't fight the wicked
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא brings up a possible challenge: a פסוק in תהלים says not to compete with evildoers, which seems to forbid challenging רשעים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if a person whispers to you, saying: But it is written, 'Do not compete with evildoers, do not be jealous of those who do wrong.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a challenge from a פסוק that seems to say the opposite. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תהלים לז, א says אל תתחר במרעים. If read simply, it means 'don't start up with bad people.' That would conflict with the rule that one may challenge רשעים.

keyTerms.meaning: Whispers to you, quietly suggests to you
Do not compete, do not get into a fight

phrases.english: And if a person whispers to you, saying:
But it is written:
'Do not compete with evildoers,
do not be jealous of those who do wrong'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם לְחָשְׁךָ אָדָם לוֹמַר וְהָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule from steps 19-20 with a פסוק that seems to disagree.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that one may challenge רשעים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: תהלים לז, א seems to say not to start up with evildoers, which contradicts משלי כח, ד.

steps.title: The verse means: don't become like them
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers that only someone with a guilty conscience says this. The real meaning of the פסוק is: don't try to be like evildoers, and don't be jealous of them so that you copy them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Tell him: Only someone whose heart bothers him says that. Rather, 'Do not compete with evildoers' means do not try to be like the evildoers. 'Do not be jealous of those who do wrong' means do not try to be like those who do wrong.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the challenge by explaining the פסוק in תהלים differently, so it no longer contradicts the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First, it says that the person asking is probably worried about his own sins, so he is afraid to stand up to others. Then it gives the real reading: אל תתחר means 'don't compete to become like them,' not 'don't fight them.' So the two פסוקים do not clash: you may fight רשעים, but you may not copy them.

keyTerms.meaning: His heart bothers him, he feels guilty

steps.whatToRemember: One may challenge רשעים. The פסוק אל תתחר במרעים only warns not to become like them.
steps.confusionAlert: Here תתחר means 'compete to be like them', not 'fight with them'. That reading is what removes the contradiction.

phrases.english: Tell him:
Only one whose heart bothers him says this.
Rather: 'Do not compete with evildoers' means
do not try to be like the evildoers;
'do not be jealous of those who do wrong' means
do not try to be like those who do wrong.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֱמוֹר לוֹ מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ נוֹקְפוֹ אוֹמֵר כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 21.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אל תתחר במרעים means 'don't fight evildoers'.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means 'don't compete to become like evildoers', so challenging רשעים is still allowed.

steps.title: A second פסוק proves what 'compete' really means
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds a פסוק from משלי: 'Do not let your heart envy sinners, but rather be in fear of ה׳ all day.' This supports its reading that the warning is about envying and copying רשעים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it also says: 'Do not let your heart envy sinners; rather, be in fear of ה׳ all the day.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is still finishing its answer from the last step. It brings a second פסוק to back up its explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 22 the ברייתא said that 'אל תתחר במרעים' means 'don't try to be like evildoers.' This פסוק uses the word קנאה (envy) in that same sense. It sets envying sinners against fearing ה׳, so the problem is copying sinners, not standing up to them.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it says': a formula that brings a second פסוק as more support
to envy, here meaning to be jealous of someone so much that you copy them

steps.whatToRemember: Up to here, the ruling of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי stands: you may challenge רשעים. The פסוקים that seem to say otherwise only warn against envying and copying them.

phrases.english: And it says: 'Let your heart not envy sinners,'

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אִם בְּיִרְאַת ה׳ כָּל הַיּוֹם״.
phrases.english: 'but rather be in fear of the Lord all the day.'
phrases.notes: The opposite of envying sinners is fearing ה׳. This shows that 'envy' here means wanting to copy them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second פסוק to support the ברייתא's reading in step 22.
steps.raayaObject: The reading that 'אל תתחר במרעים' means not to envy or copy evildoers.

steps.title: רבי יצחק says not to provoke a successful רשע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: is it really allowed to challenge רשעים? רבי יצחק taught that if a רשע's luck is shining, you should not provoke him. He brings three proofs, all from parts of one פסוק in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that really so? But רבי יצחק said: If you see a רשע whose hour is smiling on him, do not provoke him. As it says: 'His ways succeed at all times.' And more than that, he wins in judgment, as it says: 'Your judgments are far above, away from him.' And more than that, he sees the downfall of his enemies, as it says: 'All his enemies, he blows at them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rule that we may challenge רשעים. It quotes רבי יצחק, who seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן (step 19) allowed challenging רשעים. רבי יצחק says not to start up with a רשע who is enjoying success, because he will keep winning. He wins in his dealings, he wins even when judged, and he sees his enemies fall. So the two teachings seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Is that so?!' A word that opens a challenge
'But didn't he say...': brings a source that contradicts
'the hour is smiling on him': he is having good luck and success
he blows or snorts at them, meaning he defeats them easily

steps.confusionAlert: All three פסוקים quoted here are pieces of one single פסוק (תהלים י:ה). רבי יצחק is reading it phrase by phrase. These are not three separate sources.

phrases.english: Is that so?! But didn't Rabbi Yitzchak say:
If you see a wicked person
upon whom the hour is smiling,
phrases.notes: He is currently enjoying good fortune.

phrases.english: do not provoke him,
as it is said: 'His ways prosper at all times.'
And not only that, but he wins in judgment,
as it is said: 'Your judgments are far above, away from him.'
phrases.notes: Even judgment does not reach him.

phrases.english: And not only that, but he sees the downfall of his enemies,
as it is said: 'All his adversaries, he snorts at them!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתא's ruling is settled, the גמרא challenges it with a contradicting statement from an אמורא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule of רבי יוחנן and the ברייתא that one may challenge רשעים in this world.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יצחק says not to provoke a successful רשע, because he will keep winning. That seems to forbid what רבי יוחנן allowed.

steps.title: Personal matters versus matters of Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: רבי יצחק's warning is about a person's own private matters. The permission to challenge רשעים is about matters of Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one (רבי יצחק) is about his own personal matters. That one (רבי יוחנן) is about matters of Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by saying the two teachings talk about different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the fight is about your own money or honor, don't start up with a successful רשע. If the fight is for the sake of Heaven, like protesting his sins, you may challenge him. So both teachings are true, each in its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is not difficult': opens an answer that splits the cases
'This one... that one': points to each of the two teachings

steps.confusionAlert: Keep track of which הָא is which. The first הָא (personal matters) goes with רבי יצחק's 'don't provoke.' The second הָא (matters of Heaven) goes with רבי יוחנן's 'you may challenge.'

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is regarding his own matters,
that is regarding matters of Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each teaching refers to a different kind of dispute.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both teachings seemed to speak about the same situation, so they contradicted each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Don't provoke a successful רשע over personal matters. You may challenge רשעים for the sake of Heaven.

steps.title: A רשע with good luck versus one without
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: both teachings are about matters of Heaven. רבי יצחק means a רשע whose luck is shining, and רבי יוחנן means a רשע whose luck is not shining.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: both this and that are about matters of Heaven, and it is still not difficult. This one is about a רשע whom the hour is smiling on. That one is about a רשע whom the hour is not smiling on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different way to answer the same contradiction. This time the split is based on the רשע's current fortune.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer split the cases by the type of matter. This answer says that even in matters of Heaven, it is not wise to provoke a רשע who is in a lucky period, since he will win. You may challenge a רשע whose luck is not shining. רבי יצחק himself only spoke about a רשע 'שהשעה משחקת לו,' and this answer uses that detail.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you want, say': brings an alternative answer
whose hour is not smiling on him: his luck is not shining now

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to settle רבי יוחנן against רבי יצחק. (1) Personal matters versus matters of Heaven. (2) Even in matters of Heaven, a רשע with good fortune versus one without. Either way, challenging רשעים is allowed in the right situation.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
this and that are both regarding matters of Heaven,
and it is not difficult:
this is regarding a wicked person upon whom the hour is smiling,

phrases.aramaic: הָא בְּרָשָׁע שֶׁאֵין הַשָּׁעָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת לוֹ.
phrases.english: that is regarding a wicked person upon whom the hour is not smiling.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא הָא וְהָא בְּמִילֵּי דִשְׁמַיָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, alternative answer to the קשיא of step 24, instead of the split in step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative split of the cases, based on the רשע's current fortune rather than on the type of matter.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first answer said matters of Heaven are always open to challenge.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even in matters of Heaven, avoid provoking a רשע in a lucky period. You may challenge one whose luck is not shining.

steps.title: A third answer: it depends on who is doing the challenging
steps.stepSummary: Both teachings are about a רָשָׁע whose luck is shining. A צַדִּיק גָּמוּר may challenge him. A צַדִּיק who is not fully righteous may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: both teachings are about a רָשָׁע whose luck is shining, and still there is no contradiction. One teaching is about a completely righteous person, and the other is about a person who is not completely righteous.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another way to settle the conflict between רבי יצחק and רבי יוחנן. This time the difference is not about the רָשָׁע at all. It is about the person who is challenging him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 26, the difference was whether the רָשָׁע's luck was shining. Now the גמרא keeps the רָשָׁע the same in both teachings: he is lucky in both. Only a צַדִּיק גָּמוּר is safe enough to challenge him. Anyone less should hold back.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you want, say...' — this introduces another possible answer
The hour is smiling on him — he is having good fortune right now
This one and that one — both teachings

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
phrases.notes: This opens a new possible answer.

phrases.aramaic: הָא וְהָא, בְּרָשָׁע שֶׁהַשָּׁעָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת לוֹ,
phrases.english: this and that are both about a wicked person on whom the hour is smiling,
phrases.notes: Both רבי יצחק and רבי יוחנן are talking about a lucky רָשָׁע.

phrases.english: and still it is not difficult:
this one is about a completely righteous person,
phrases.notes: He may challenge the רָשָׁע (רבי יוחנן).

phrases.english: that one is about a righteous person who is not complete.
phrases.notes: He should not challenge the רָשָׁע (רבי יצחק).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא, בְּרָשָׁע שֶׁהַשָּׁעָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a third answer to the קשיא of step 24. It is an alternative to the answers in steps 25 and 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between cases, based on the level of the person who challenges
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both teachings seem to clash about challenging the same lucky רָשָׁע.
steps.terutzMaskana: A צַדִּיק גָּמוּר may challenge even a lucky רָשָׁע. A צַדִּיק who is not fully righteous may not.

steps.title: רב הונא's פסוק: the wicked swallows one more righteous than he
steps.stepSummary: Support comes from רב הונא, who reads a פסוק in חבקוק about a רָשָׁע swallowing a צַדִּיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב הונא said: what is the meaning of the פסוק, 'Why do You look at traitors and stay silent, when the wicked swallows one more righteous than he?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from רב הונא for the idea that some righteous people can be harmed by a רָשָׁע. This step sets up a question about the פסוק that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'צַדִּיק מִמֶּנּוּ' (more righteous than he) will turn out to be the key. They hint that the victim is only better than the רָשָׁע, not perfectly righteous. First, though, the גמרא will question the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written?

phrases.english: As Rav Huna said:
What is the meaning of what is written:
'Why do You look on those who act treacherously,
and stay silent when the wicked swallows
one more righteous than he?'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This brings a source to back up the distinction made in step 27.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a צַדִּיק who is not fully righteous can be harmed by a רָשָׁע

steps.title: Can a wicked person really swallow a righteous one?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא challenges the פסוק using two other פסוקים that say a צַדִּיק is protected.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can a wicked person really swallow a righteous person? But it is written, 'ה׳ will not leave him in his hand,' and it is written, 'No harm will happen to the righteous.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא asks how a רָשָׁע could ever destroy a צַדִּיק. Other פסוקים promise that a צַדִּיק is protected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in חבקוק seems to clash with תהלים 37:33 and משלי 12:21. Those two פסוקים say that ה׳ protects the צַדִּיק from harm. So who exactly is the 'righteous' person in חבקוק who gets swallowed?

keyTerms.meaning: Is it really so? (a surprised question)
But isn't it written...? (introduces a contradicting verse)
Will not happen to, will not befall

phrases.english: Does a wicked person really swallow a righteous one?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא כְּתִיב: ה׳ לֹא יַעַזְבֶנּוּ בְיָדוֹ,
phrases.english: But it is written: 'The Lord will not leave him in his hand,'
and it is written: 'No harm shall befall the righteous.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי רָשָׁע בּוֹלֵעַ צַדִּיק? וְהָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This questions the plain meaning of the פסוק quoted in step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain reading of חבקוק 1:13, that a רָשָׁע swallows a צַדִּיק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Other פסוקים promise that a צַדִּיק is protected, so a רָשָׁע should not be able to swallow him.

steps.title: Only someone 'more righteous than he' gets swallowed
steps.stepSummary: A רָשָׁע can swallow someone who is only better than he is. He cannot swallow a צַדִּיק גָּמוּר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: someone who is only 'more righteous than he,' the רָשָׁע swallows. A completely righteous person he does not swallow.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers his own question by reading the exact words 'צַדִּיק מִמֶּנּוּ' carefully. This answer proves the distinction made in step 27.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק does not say just 'a צַדִּיק.' It says 'more righteous than he,' meaning only better by comparison. That kind of person can be hurt. A צַדִּיק גָּמוּר cannot, so he is the one who may safely challenge a lucky רָשָׁע.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather — this introduces the corrected reading

steps.confusionAlert: 'צַדִּיק מִמֶּנּוּ' does NOT mean a great צַדִּיק. It means someone who is only more righteous than this רָשָׁע. He may still be far from perfect.
steps.whatToRemember: A צַדִּיק גָּמוּר is protected even from a lucky רָשָׁע, so he may challenge him. A person who is only 'better than the רָשָׁע' is not protected.

phrases.english: Rather: one who is only more righteous than he, he swallows;
a completely righteous person, he does not swallow.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This answers the קשיא of step 29 and completes the proof for step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the exact wording of the פסוק closely
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק seems to say that a רָשָׁע can destroy any צַדִּיק.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a partly righteous person can be swallowed. A צַדִּיק גָּמוּר cannot.

steps.title: Another answer: when luck smiles on the wicked, things are different
steps.stepSummary: A second answer to רב הונא's question: usually a רָשָׁע cannot harm a צַדִּיק, but when his luck is shining, he can.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: when the hour is smiling on the רָשָׁע, it is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to explain how the פסוק in חבקוק fits with the promises that a צַדִּיק is protected.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this answer, the protection promised in תהלים and משלי holds in normal times. When a רָשָׁע is having a time of strong good fortune, even a צַדִּיק can be harmed. Here the deciding factor is the רָשָׁע's luck, not how righteous the victim is.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different — this is a special case

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
when the hour is smiling on him, it is different.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, שָׁעָה מְשַׂחֶקֶת לוֹ — שָׁאנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is a second answer to the קשיא in step 29. It is an alternative to step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: An exception based on a special time
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The promised protection of the צַדִּיק seems to clash with the פסוק in חבקוק.
steps.terutzMaskana: The protection is the normal rule. A רָשָׁע whose luck is shining is an exception.

steps.title: Setting a fixed place for prayer makes your enemies fall
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that someone who sets a fixed place for his תְּפִלָּה will see his enemies fall beneath him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: anyone who sets a fixed place for his prayer, his enemies fall beneath him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new teaching by רבי יוחנן. This one is about having a set place for תְּפִלָּה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new topic, connected to the earlier teachings mainly because the same speaker said them. The claim is that keeping a fixed place for תְּפִלָּה brings protection from enemies. The source comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: One who sets a fixed place

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the well-known practice of having a מָקוֹם קָבוּעַ, a fixed place for davening.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said
in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:
Anyone who sets a fixed place for his prayer,
his enemies fall beneath him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This starts a new teaching in the series of statements by רבי יוחנן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setting a fixed place for תְּפִלָּה causes one's enemies to fall.

steps.title: The verse: 'I will set a place for My people'
steps.stepSummary: The source is a פסוק in שמואל ב: ה׳ will set a 'place' for ישראל, and wicked people will no longer afflict them.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'I will set a place for My people ישראל, and I will plant them, and they will dwell in their place. They will not be disturbed anymore, and wicked people will no longer afflict them as before.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the פסוק that proves רבי יוחנן's teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is built on the word 'מָקוֹם' (place) in the פסוק. That word is read as a hint to a fixed place for תְּפִלָּה. The end of the פסוק, 'wicked people will no longer afflict them,' matches the promise that one's enemies will fall.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.english: As it is said: 'And I will set a place for My people Israel,'
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 7:10. The word 'place' is the key to the proof.

phrases.english: and I will plant them, and they will dwell in their place,
and they will be disturbed no more,
and the wicked will no longer
afflict them as at first.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This gives the source for step 32.
steps.raayaObject: A fixed place for תְּפִלָּה protects a person from enemies

steps.title: רב הונא notices two different words in parallel פסוקים
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא points out that שמואל says 'לְעַנּוֹתוֹ' (to afflict him), while the parallel פסוק in דברי הימים says 'לְכַלּוֹתוֹ' (to destroy him).
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא raised a contradiction: one פסוק says 'to afflict him,' and another says 'to destroy him.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא notices that the same פסוק appears in two books of תנ״ך with a different word. This step sets up the question, and step 35 answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל ב 7:10 says 'לְעַנּוֹתוֹ' (afflict). The same promise in דברי הימים א 17:9 says 'לְכַלּוֹתוֹ' (destroy). Since it is one promise, why are the words different? The גמרא will explain this next.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised a contradiction (set two sources against each other)

phrases.english: Rav Huna raised a contradiction:
it is written 'to afflict him,'
and it is written 'to destroy him.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The פסוק quoted in step 33 leads רב הונא to compare it with its parallel version.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of the promise in שמואל ב 7:10 compared with דברי הימים א 17:9
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two versions of the same promise use different words, 'afflict' and 'destroy.' This needs an explanation.

steps.title: First they afflict, in the end they destroy
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the contradiction between שמואל (לְעַנּוֹתוֹ) and דברי הימים (לְכַלּוֹתוֹ). Both words are true, because they describe two stages of the enemy's plan.
steps.simpleTranslation: At the beginning, the enemy wants to afflict; in the end, the enemy wants to destroy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב הונא's question from step 34. The two פסוקים are not arguing; each one describes a different stage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל describes the enemy's first goal, which is to cause suffering. דברי הימים describes his final goal, which is to wipe ישראל out completely. So the promise of a 'place' protects ישראל from both stages.
steps.whatToRemember: The two פסוקים describe two stages: affliction first, destruction later.

phrases.english: At first — to afflict him,
and in the end — to destroy him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the wording contradiction raised in step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two stages in time: each פסוק describes a different phase of the enemy's intent.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two פסוקים seem to give conflicting descriptions of what the wicked do.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both descriptions are correct. The enemy first afflicts and later aims to destroy.

steps.title: Serving Torah is greater than studying it
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחי, teaches that serving a Torah scholar is greater than learning Torah from him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: serving Torah is greater than studying it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from the same pair of רבי יוחנן and רבי שמעון בן יוחי. It is about the value of serving a תַּלְמִיד חָכָם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Studying gives you the words of Torah. Serving a scholar lets you watch how he lives every part of life by the Torah. That is why serving is ranked higher.

keyTerms.meaning: Serving Torah, meaning personally attending to a Torah scholar

steps.confusionAlert: 'שימוש' here does not mean 'using' the Torah. It means serving a Torah scholar and spending time with him.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:
Greater is the service of Torah
than its study,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching in the series of statements by רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Serving a Torah scholar is greater than learning Torah from him.

steps.title: Proof from אלישע pouring water for אליהו
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק praises אלישע as the one who 'poured water' on אליהו's hands, not as the one who 'learned' from him. This shows that service is greater.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'Here is אלישע son of שפט, who poured water on the hands of אליהו.' The פסוק does not say 'learned'; it says 'poured.' This teaches that serving is greater than studying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for the teaching in step 36. It points to the exact word the פסוק chose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the פסוק wants to describe אלישע's greatness, it could have said he learned from אליהו. Instead, it says he poured water for him, which is an act of service. The choice of word shows that service is the higher praise.

phrases.english: as it is stated: 'Here is Elisha son of Shafat,

phrases.aramaic: אֲשֶׁר יָצַק מַיִם עַל יְדֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ״.
phrases.english: who poured water on the hands of Elijah.'
'Learned' is not stated, but rather 'poured' —
this teaches that its service is greater than its study.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״פֹּה אֱלִישָׁע בֶּן שָׁפָט אֲשֶׁר יָצַק מַיִם עַל יְדֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the scriptural source for step 36.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that serving Torah is greater than studying it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מלכים ב ג:יא, where אלישע is described as the one who poured water on אליהו's hands.

steps.title: Why didn't you come to shul to daven?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק asks רב נחמן why he did not come to the בית כנסת to daven. רב נחמן answers that he was not able to.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק said to רב נחמן: Why didn't the Master come to the בית כנסת to pray? He answered: I was not able to.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. It sets up another teaching of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי, which comes at the end of the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יצחק notices that רב נחמן was missing from communal תפילה. רב נחמן explains that he was too weak to come, so his absence was not a lack of caring.

keyTerms.meaning: Master, a respectful way to say 'you'

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יִצְחָק לְרַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzḥak said to Rav Naḥman:
What is the reason the Master did not come
to the synagogue to pray?
He said to him: I was not able.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא לָא אָתֵי מָר לְבֵי כְּנִישְׁתָּא לְצַלּוֹיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story that leads into the next teaching of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רב נחמן was absent from communal תפילה.

steps.title: Then gather ten men at home
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק suggests that רב נחמן gather a מנין at his home and daven there.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Let the Master gather ten men and pray.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק pushes back on the excuse. If you cannot get to shul, bring the מנין to you.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The excuse 'I could not come' only explains why רב נחמן missed the building. It does not explain why he missed davening with ten. So רבי יצחק offers a way to still daven with a מנין.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לִכַּנְפִי לְמָר עַשְׂרָה וְלִיצַלֵּי.
phrases.english: He said to him: Let the Master gather ten and pray.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's excuse from step 38 by offering an alternative.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's excuse that he could not come to shul.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being unable to travel does not prevent davening with a מנין at home.

steps.title: It is too much of a burden
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that gathering a מנין at his home is too burdensome.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The matter is burdensome for me.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן turns down the suggestion. He does not want to trouble ten people to come to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is not that he cannot get ten men. He feels it is wrong to impose on the community to come to his house for his sake.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter is burdensome or troublesome for me

phrases.english: He said to him: The matter is burdensome for me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Deflects the suggestion made in step 39.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical objection: the suggestion places too much of a burden on others.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Gathering ten men at home solves the problem.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is too much trouble to impose on others, so that option is rejected.

steps.title: Have the שליח ציבור tell you when the צבור davens
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק offers another option. A messenger should come and tell רב נחמן when the community is davening, so he can daven at the same time at home.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let the Master tell the community's messenger: at the time the community prays, he should come and let the Master know.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יצחק offers a third solution that does not burden anyone. רב נחמן can daven at home at the same moment the צבור davens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he cannot go to shul and will not bring a מנין home, he can at least match his תפילה to the time of the communal תפילה. Notice that רבי יצחק keeps searching for some way to connect רב נחמן to the צבור's davening.

keyTerms.meaning: Messenger of the community, or the שליח ציבור

phrases.english: And let the Master tell the messenger of the congregation,
that at the time the congregation prays
he should come and inform the Master.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the מנין idea is rejected, רבי יצחק offers a new solution.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's continued avoidance of communal תפילה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even without a מנין, he can daven at the same time as the צבור without burdening anyone.

steps.title: Why all this effort?
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן asks רבי יצחק why he is working so hard to get him to daven when the צבור davens.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What is all this?
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן asks why it matters so much. This question sets up the teaching that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יצחק's three suggestions show that he believes there is something special about davening together with the צבור. רב נחמן wants to know the source of that belief.

phrases.english: He said to him: What is all this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רבי יצחק's repeated suggestions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason why davening at the time of the צבור is so important.

steps.title: רבי יצחק begins quoting רבי יוחנן's source
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק answers by starting to quote a teaching of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי. The teaching itself appears on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Because רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. רבי יצחק is introducing the teaching that explains his effort, and the actual words of that teaching come on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole story was a frame for this teaching. Its content, which explains why the time of communal תפילה matters, continues right after this line.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for the answer on this amud. The teaching itself is in the next lines of the גמרא.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: He said to him: Because Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 42 by citing a source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The reason is a teaching of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי, which continues on the next amud.
